claims.text: Menu is designed wheat-free and sweets are all 米粉, but it is a shared working kitchen/bar with beer on premises; no dedicated GF equipment documented.
Kitchen uses mostly wheat-free seasonings, but its soy sauce contains a minute amount of wheat; wheat-allergic diners are advised to phone ahead (076-224-8787) to confirm safe options.
Casein-free but includes goat cheese, meat and fish; not a vegan kitchen.
Dietitian-supervised, allergy-responsive menu; staff invite wheat-allergic guests to call ahead to confirm safe dishes.
「料理は全てグルテン・カゼイン・エッグフリー」- all dishes gluten-, casein- and egg-free; all sweets are rice flour.
Galettes are made with buckwheat (soba) flour from a heritage Echizen variety, a grain that is naturally free of wheat.

This is a ramen shop whose bowls are built on homemade, medium-thick curly wheat noodles, so the broth and serving area are inherently wheat-heavy. It should not be considered celiac-safe, and no source documents a gluten-free noodle, a separate gluten-free prep area, or any cross-contamination controls. Celiac diners should confirm directly before visiting.
The other house specialty, gyukatsu, is breaded and deep-fried, which adds wheat flour/breadcrumbs and frying-oil cross-contact to the kitchen. No source confirms whether a dedicated fryer is used.

No source specifies the soy sauce or seasonings used. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and the spicy 'Volcano' broth is built on an original spicy miso (miso can also contain wheat/barley), so gluten-free diners should assume wheat is present in the seasonings unless staff confirm otherwise.

A vegan ramen option is advertised, but no source describes how it is prepared relative to the wagyu and beef-bone-broth dishes. Strict vegans should ask whether the vegan bowl is cooked with separate pots, utensils, and noodle water, since none of that is documented.

The kitchen is pork-free and oriented around halal preparation, and the menu explicitly includes vegan options, so the staff are accustomed to accommodating dietary restrictions and are a reasonable group to discuss your needs with directly.
The Kawaramachi location lists a vegan option directly on its profile, signaling that plant-based requests are part of normal service rather than an unusual ask.

Described by sources as a 100% gluten-free café, meaning the whole kitchen is dedicated gluten-free rather than offering GF items alongside wheat ones. This greatly reduces cross-contamination risk, but specific protocols are not documented, so celiac diners should still confirm directly.
The signature canelé and baked goods are made with rice flour in place of wheat flour, consistent with a flour-free (wheat-free) kitchen.

This is a sweets-focused bakery and café (canelés, cakes, puddings, cookies, afternoon tea), not a savory shokudo. No soy-sauce-based dishes are documented; if any savory items are added, ask whether wheat-free (gluten-free) soy sauce is used, since most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
A dedicated, fully gluten-free café where everything on offer is gluten-free, so there is no wheat flour in the kitchen to cross-contaminate with.
Baked goods are also low-sugar or sugar-free, with sweetness from plant-based ingredients instead of refined sugar.

The signature vegan burger is served on a homemade bun made from wheat flour and whole wheat flour, so the burger as served is not gluten-free. Wheat is baked in-house, which means flour is handled in the kitchen.

Some components are naturally gluten-free in themselves - the patty is chickpea-paste based, and the kitchen also offers salad-style and bowl dishes (Buddha bowl, bibimbap) - but no dedicated gluten-free preparation or cross-contamination controls are documented. Celiac diners should confirm directly with the owner before ordering.

No specific soy sauce or seasoning ingredient details are documented. As is typical in Japan, any soy sauce used likely contains wheat unless confirmed otherwise, so wheat-sensitive and celiac diners should ask about sauces and seasonings.
Vegginy is a fully vegan kitchen - the entire menu is plant-based with no animal products on premises - so animal cross-contact is not a concern. The bun uses soy milk rather than dairy.

Reviewers describe the staff as very friendly and the owner as passionate about her work and a great English speaker, which should make it easy to ask about ingredients and accommodations. No specific allergy-handling protocol is documented, so discuss your needs directly when ordering.
Fully vegan kitchen, so no risk of animal-product cross-contact; the menu is entirely plant-based.
Friendly, English-speaking owner who is hands-on and passionate, making it straightforward to discuss ingredients and dietary needs.
Food is made largely from scratch - homemade buns, patties, and baked goods - so the owner knows the ingredients in each dish.

This is one of the rare ramen shops that takes gluten-free seriously: it offers a dedicated gluten-free ramen lineup (and a gluten-free omakase set) rather than just removing items, which is unusual for a wheat-heavy dish like ramen.
Reviewers report the kitchen uses separate cooking water for the gluten-free noodles and prepares allergy meals carefully.

It is not a fully dedicated gluten-free facility — gluten-free items run alongside regular wheat ramen — so some cross-contact risk remains in a shared kitchen. One reviewer flagged a concern about cross-contamination from wooden ramen spoons.

Reports on the fryer are mixed: at one location staff confirmed a separate fryer, while another review noted no dedicated fryer — so confirm fryer arrangements for fried items at the specific location before ordering.

The kitchen specifically uses gluten-free soy sauce for its gyoza and dim sum, which directly addresses the usual problem that most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Still confirm gluten-free soy is used on any dish you order, as standard wheat-based soy sauce is common in Japanese kitchens.

Vegan ramen is a core offering built on kelp, miso, and soy sauce rather than meat or fish stock, but it is prepared in the same kitchen that handles wagyu and other meats, so strict vegans should confirm separate handling.
Staff ask about allergies and intolerances when you order and reportedly understand what celiac disease means, which is notable for a Japanese ramen shop.
The reservation process explicitly invites guests to flag any food allergies or intolerances in advance.
A reviewer described the team as super sharp about celiac, cross-contamination, and safe preparation practices.
Widely praised as one of the best gluten-free ramen experiences in Kyoto, with reviewers saying the gluten-free ramen and dumplings tasted amazing.
Gluten-free and vegan items are clearly available across the menu, with the shop offering good choices for many diets.
Despite ramen being a wheat-heavy dish, this kitchen was built around inclusive dining and treats gluten-free and vegan guests as a primary audience rather than an afterthought.

name: MOON and BACK Ramen Bar & Brunch

claims.text: The kitchen builds its gluten-free ramen on special rice-based noodles developed specifically to be wheat-free, rather than swapping noodles in a shared wheat-ramen line, which lowers a major source of gluten cross-contact for a ramen shop.

A gluten-free guide lists the venue as celiac friendly with low risk of cross-contamination and notes the use of dedicated appliances for gluten-free preparation; this is community-reported, not formal third-party certification, so confirm current practice with staff.

The restaurant's own site and listings do not spell out kitchen-level protocols such as a dedicated fryer, separate noodle-boiling water, or separate utensils, so celiac diners should ask directly about these specifics before ordering.

For the vegan and gluten-free bowls the kitchen uses a custom-blended miso and soy sauce rather than standard ramen seasoning; the site does not explicitly state the soy sauce is wheat-free or gluten-free, so celiac diners should confirm the soy sauce used in their specific dish.

The vegan ramen is described as completely free from any animal ingredients, built on naturally fermented miso and soy milk. However, the same kitchen also cooks Wagyu, teriyaki chicken, and other meat dishes, so vegans concerned about shared equipment or cross-contact should confirm preparation with staff.
The restaurant asks guests to let them know about any food allergies or intolerances when booking, indicating they collect allergy information at reservation.
A gluten-free guide reports the venue has staff knowledgeable about celiac safety and offers a gluten-free omakase set with careful service for gluten-sensitive guests.

This is a rare ramen specialist designed from the ground up for gluten-free and vegan diners, with dedicated wheat-free rice noodles and a fully plant-based bowl, making it far more accommodating than a typical wheat-and-dashi ramen shop.
Guests with wheat allergies and gluten intolerance are explicitly welcomed, and reviewers praise the gluten-free ramen and dumplings, with some calling it the best gluten-free ramen they have found.

The cafe is fully plant-based and offers a number of gluten-free items, including smoothie bowls, rice-flour muffins, cakes and cookies. No information on shared prep surfaces or flour-dust cross-contamination is published, so a strict celiac should confirm preparation directly with staff before ordering.

This is a smoothie- and baked-goods-focused vegan cafe rather than a savory soy-sauce kitchen; documented menus emphasize fruit, vegetable and spice smoothies, soups, vegan bread and rice-flour baked goods. No specific soy-sauce details are published. Soy milk and amazake do appear in several smoothies, which is relevant for soy-sensitive diners.
The menu is described as 100 percent vegan and plant-based, with all items additive-free, so animal-product cross-contact risk is low.

A diner with a nut allergy reported a serious incident: a smoothie bowl arrived garnished with visible walnuts, and after sending it back, staff offered only to scoop the nuts out rather than remake the dish, assuring him it was 'just the garnish.' He nonetheless had an allergic reaction, with nuts apparently present in the bowl or an accompanying cookie. The reviewer felt the cafe did not show due diligence in guiding a nut-allergy sufferer through the menu.

Nuts are used heavily across the menu - nut milks, walnut and granola smoothie-bowl toppings, and nut-studded muffins - so anyone with a nut allergy should be explicit with staff and exercise strong caution.
A reviewer noted the cafe offers many kinds of gluten-free muffins.
Fully vegan kitchen using additive-free, plant-based, organic and pesticide-free ingredients, which simplifies things for plant-based diners.
